draft.title: Variation in populations
card: A gene can have different versions, called alleles. Allele frequency is how common one allele is among all the copies of that gene in a population.
Frequency is a fraction or a percentage. If 30 of every 100 copies of a gene are allele B, the frequency of B is 0.3, or 30%. The frequencies of all alleles of a gene add to 1.
Frequency counts alleles, not individuals. A population can have many people showing a trait while the allele for it is rare, or the reverse.
Genetic testing and DNA sequencing read the alleles that people carry. Scientists can then count them across many people to measure the variation in a population.
draft.remember: Allele frequency is the share of all copies of a gene that are one allele, and DNA tests let us count it.

a.q: In a population of 100 people, each person carries 2 copies of a gene. Allele R appears in 40 of the 200 copies. What is the frequency of R?
a.why: Frequency is the copies of R divided by all copies of the gene: 40 ÷ 200 = 0.2. The figure 0.4 is tempting, but it divides by the 100 people instead of the 200 copies.
a.clue: Count copies of the gene, not people.

b.q: A lab sequences one gene in 500 people in a town and finds 1000 copies of it. Allele T makes up 0.15 of them. Which statement is correct?
opts: There are 150 copies of T, and the other alleles total 0.85
There are 75 copies of T, and the other alleles total 0.85
There are 150 copies of T, and the other alleles total 0.15
There are 75 copies of T, and the other alleles total 0.15
b.why: 0.15 × 1000 copies = 150 copies of T. All alleles of a gene add to 1, so the others total 1 - 0.15 = 0.85. Using 500 people gives 75, but frequency is a share of gene copies, not of people.
b.clue: Each person has two copies, and all frequencies add to 1.

b.best: There are 150 copies of T, and the other alleles total 0.85

problems.detail: 'A population can have many people showing a trait while the allele for it is rare' is misleading. If an allele is rare, few people carry it, so few can show its trait; at most about twice the allele frequency, even when it is dominant. Only 'the reverse' holds well: a common recessive allele with few people showing it. Reword, for example: 'An allele can be fairly common while few people show its trait, because many carry only one copy of a recessive allele.'

check.summary: Both questions and their explanations are correct. One card line wrongly suggests a rare allele can produce a trait in many people, and it should be reworded.
